concepts.name: extended reality
concepts.definition: Extended reality (XR) is an umbrella term, not a specific technology, that covers all present or future immersive technologies, such as augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), and mixed reality (MR).

defining_facts.text: Extended Reality (XR) is an umbrella term, not a specific technology, that covers all present or future immersive technologies, such as augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), and mixed reality (MR).

The X in Extended Reality (XR) can be read as a variable, not only as part of 'extended', and its values such as A, V, and M denote augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), and mixed reality (MR), while its many possible values form present or future immersive technologies.

Although adoption statistics can be misleading, earlier use forecasts discussed in the course indicate that extended reality, which covers augmented reality (AR) and virtual reality (VR), has commercial potential in video games (about 34% or more than one third of applications), healthcare, engineering, live events, video entertainment, real estate, retail, and military (about 4% of application areas, a figure that may change); because worldwide military budgets are huge, even 4% is a large monetary amount, so penetration in the commercial space can be expected both percentage-wise and value-wise.

concepts.name: virtual reality
concepts.definition: Virtual reality (VR) is an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli provided by a computer, in which a person's actions partially determine what happens and which replaces the user's sense of reality without requiring the physical existence of objects or places.

defining_facts.text: Virtual reality (VR) is, according to the Miriam Webster dictionary, an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli, in which sights and sounds play a primary role and are provided by a computer, possibly along with other sensory stimuli, and in which a person's actions partially determine what happens in the environment.
Augmented reality (AR) alters the ongoing perception of the real world, whereas virtual reality (VR) completely replaces the user's sense of reality with a virtual environment.

A virtual reality (VR) system does not require the physical existence of an object or place, because it creates a virtual environment, whereas an augmented reality (AR) or mixed reality (MR) system requires the place being experienced to exist.

The early era in the historical evolution of virtual reality (VR) is the period before modern digital computers were developed in the 1940s, and although not everything was present in that era, a few key developments were conceptually similar to immersive virtual reality experiences.

In virtual reality (VR), headsets or display devices present two-dimensional (2D) images, but stereoscopic vision makes the user perceive them as three-dimensional (3D) objects and space, which is immersion.

The flight simulator concept introduced for the first time in 1928 by Edwin A. Link evolved into sophisticated flight simulators with multiple sensors that provide an immersive experience, and this early development is considered a precursor to modern multi-sensory immersive virtual reality (VR).

The main objective of any virtual reality (VR) system is to let the user experience an artificial environment through sensory stimuli provided by the computer, not only for sight and sound but for all sensory organs.

There are broadly two major issues in experiencing virtual reality (VR): the technological issue of how to generate suitable sensory stimuli for the artificial environment, and the psychological issue of how to perceive those stimuli suitably, a human-factor issue that technology does not address and that is likely to differ between users.

The technological and psychological issues in virtual reality (VR) give rise to two major concerns that appear in almost every literature on VR technology or experience, namely immersion and presence.
The causes of cyber sickness are broadly internal factors and external factors, and external factors comprise hardware and virtual reality (VR) content.

Cyber sickness can be independent of age when users view general virtual reality (VR) content, while age may be a factor for controllable content, making the age relationship clearer for controllable content.

A possible reason for increased cyber sickness among female head-mounted display (HMD) users is inter-pupillary distance (IPD) fit, because IPD determines stereoscopic vision and a greater proportion of females may have trouble finding a good fit; this implies virtual reality (VR) displays should have a wider IPD adjustable range for female users.

Virtual reality (VR) recreates realistic movement and visual environments, making the user feel as if in a real-world environment; therefore, users with motion sickness (MS) susceptibility tend also to have cyber sickness susceptibility.

Prior exposure to virtual reality (VR) systems and repeated exposure to VR can reduce the effect of motion sickness (MS) susceptibility on cyber sickness and reduce cyber sickness severity over time, so the positive correlation may not hold if either or both conditions are satisfied.

A user's physical position affects cyber sickness susceptibility: using a virtual reality (VR) system in a standing posture is likely to induce more cyber sickness, or more severe cyber sickness, than using the same system while sitting.

A virtual reality (VR) system is designed to create interactions that make the user feel immersed, and the amount of presence and the quality of the overall experience depend on fooling the user's perceptual system into believing the virtual system is the familiar real world.
Virtual reality generally provides the brain with sensory signals that are inconsistent with the user's real-life experiences and behavior.

One possible outcome of generally inconsistent virtual reality stimulation is that the body adapts to the new stimuli, making the user unaware of any flaws in the system and causing the user to believe that the virtual system is the real world rather than an artificial system.

Another possible outcome of generally inconsistent virtual reality stimulation is that the body may not be able to adapt, causing increased fatigue or headaches, and this non-adaptation may lead to cyber sickness, that is, dizziness, nausea, or a large set of different symptoms experienced while using virtual reality systems.
An understanding of human perception is needed to design a better virtual reality (VR) system or to identify and resolve flaws in a given system.

In the Unity editor interface, the preference tab lets the developer select extended reality (XR) settings for three system types: virtual reality, which simulates a completely artificial environment around the user; mixed reality, which combines Unity's own environment with the user's real world environment and allows the environments to interact; and augmented reality, which provides layers of content over a digital view of the real world.

concepts.name: augmented reality
concepts.definition: Augmented reality (AR) is an enhanced version of reality created by technology, in which computer-generated digital content is overlaid on the real world in real time and registered in 3D, so the user perceives and interacts with the enhanced environment.

defining_facts.text: Augmented reality on the reality-virtuality continuum is the intermediate state in which the real environment is augmented with virtual content.
Augmented virtuality on the reality-virtuality continuum is the intermediate state, opposite augmented reality, in which the virtual environment is augmented with real-world content.
Augmented reality (AR), unlike virtual reality (VR), does not require an immersive experience and instead emphasizes augmenting real-world content with digital content.
Augmented reality (AR) applications include archaeology, architecture, industrial manufacturing, commerce (particularly e-commerce), gaming, and medical domains, among other domains.
In archaeology, augmented reality (AR) can display things that are not visible to the naked eye on a screen and can reconstruct lost structures.
In industrial manufacturing, augmented reality (AR) can allow a person to see things while repairing or troubleshooting a component of an industrial setup.
The presence of many augmented reality (AR) applications in commerce, particularly e-commerce, is one motivation for the metaverse concept.
Pokemon Go is a famous augmented reality (AR) gaming application.

Augmented reality (AR) is defined by the Merriam-Webster dictionary as an enhanced version of reality created by the use of technology, primarily computer technology, to overlay digital information on an image of something being viewed through a device.

The systemic definition of augmented reality (AR) states that an AR system should have three characteristics: combining the real world with virtual content, being interactive in real time so that interaction with the digital content added to the real-world view is reflected immediately, and being registered in 3D.

An augmented reality (AR) system has four characteristics: it enhances the real world with computer-generated digital content such as image, video, or text; the enhancement is registered in 3D so that it appears at its appropriate place rather than randomly and mixes seamlessly with real-world objects; the enhancement is experienced through the user's sensory organs; and the system supports the user's interaction with the digital content in the enhanced environment rather than separately, giving the user the feel of being in reality at all times.

A system is identified as an augmented reality (AR) system by checking the four AR characteristics one by one, and it is an AR system only if all four are satisfied; if at least one characteristic is not satisfied, it is not an AR system.
Augmented reality (AR) alters the ongoing perception of the real world, whereas virtual reality (VR) completely replaces the user's sense of reality with a virtual environment.

A virtual reality (VR) system does not require the physical existence of an object or place, because it creates a virtual environment, whereas an augmented reality (AR) or mixed reality (MR) system requires the place being experienced to exist.
An augmented reality (AR) system can superimpose extra information, such as non-existent furniture, as digital content over the real-world view of a room.

The dictionary definition of mixed reality (MR) describes MR as a medium consisting of immersive computer-generated environments in which elements of physical and virtual environments are combined, but this definition is not categorical about how MR differs from virtual reality (VR) or augmented reality (AR).

One definition of mixed reality (MR) is that MR comprises everything in between the two extremes of the reality-virtuality continuum, the real environment and the virtual environment, so augmented reality (AR) is included in this broader definition of MR.

Another definition of mixed reality (MR) is that MR denotes the capability to combine augmented reality (AR) and virtual reality (VR) technologies in the same application or on the same device, so such a combined application is called MR from a developer's point of view.

Another definition of mixed reality (MR) describes MR as a strong version of augmented reality (AR), meaning a more capable version of augmented reality that has an advanced understanding of the physical environment and may be bound to specific hardware.

In one definition used by many people, mixed reality (MR) is a synonym for augmented reality (AR), because in both cases the user views reality augmented or enhanced with digital content overlaid on the view of reality, and can interact with that content.

Because most definitions of mixed reality (MR) are confusing and the controversy is not needed for this course, the course assumes that MR is the same technology as augmented reality (AR) and treats the two terms as interchangeable.

In the Unity editor interface, the preference tab lets the developer select extended reality (XR) settings for three system types: virtual reality, which simulates a completely artificial environment around the user; mixed reality, which combines Unity's own environment with the user's real world environment and allows the environments to interact; and augmented reality, which provides layers of content over a digital view of the real world.

concepts.name: mixed reality
concepts.definition: Mixed reality (MR) is an immersive technology that is the same as augmented reality, in which digital content is overlaid on the view of reality and can be interacted with.

defining_facts.text: Mixed reality, in a broad sense, is the entire space between the real environment extreme and the virtual environment extreme of the reality-virtuality continuum, containing different degrees of augmentation of the real environment with virtual content and of the virtual environment with real content.
There is no agreement among practitioners and in the literature on the precise definition of mixed reality (MR).

The dictionary definition of mixed reality (MR) describes MR as a medium consisting of immersive computer-generated environments in which elements of physical and virtual environments are combined, but this definition is not categorical about how MR differs from virtual reality (VR) or augmented reality (AR).

One definition of mixed reality (MR) is that MR comprises everything in between the two extremes of the reality-virtuality continuum, the real environment and the virtual environment, so augmented reality (AR) is included in this broader definition of MR.

Another definition of mixed reality (MR) is that MR denotes the capability to combine augmented reality (AR) and virtual reality (VR) technologies in the same application or on the same device, so such a combined application is called MR from a developer's point of view.

Another definition of mixed reality (MR) describes MR as a strong version of augmented reality (AR), meaning a more capable version of augmented reality that has an advanced understanding of the physical environment and may be bound to specific hardware.

In one definition used by many people, mixed reality (MR) is a synonym for augmented reality (AR), because in both cases the user views reality augmented or enhanced with digital content overlaid on the view of reality, and can interact with that content.

Because most definitions of mixed reality (MR) are confusing and the controversy is not needed for this course, the course assumes that MR is the same technology as augmented reality (AR) and treats the two terms as interchangeable.

In the Unity editor interface, the preference tab lets the developer select extended reality (XR) settings for three system types: virtual reality, which simulates a completely artificial environment around the user; mixed reality, which combines Unity's own environment with the user's real world environment and allows the environments to interact; and augmented reality, which provides layers of content over a digital view of the real world.

concepts.name: virtual environment
concepts.definition: Virtual environment is a non-real, computer-generated graphical representation of a real or imaginary world, populated with artificial objects, that is experienced through computer-generated sensory stimuli.

defining_facts.text: A virtual reality (VR) system is defined by three characteristics: an artificial or synthetic environment, sensory experience through computer-generated stimuli, and user actions that partially determine what happens in the environment; a system with these aspects can be categorized as a virtual reality system and distinguished from other systems, which are not supposed to have these aspects.

The artificial or synthetic environment of a virtual reality (VR) system is a computer-generated graphical representation of a real world or an imaginary or fantastic world, populated with artificial objects, and is not a real environment.

An artificial environment in a virtual reality (VR) system can recreate a real world using real-world imagery or video, as in a virtual tour, but it still counts as a virtual reality system because it is a computer-generated scenario and changes are not happening in real time.

The sensory experience characteristic of a virtual reality (VR) system means that the system provides computer-generated stimuli to the user's sensory organs, such as eyes and ears, so the user can immersively experience the artificial or synthetic environment, and this immersive experience is a hallmark of a virtual reality system.

The user interaction characteristic of a virtual reality (VR) system means that the system must be interactive: the user can act on or interact with elements in the environment, and user actions or inputs partially determine what happens in the environment, producing dynamic changes in the virtual environment, just as people interact with objects in the real world.

concepts.name: immersion
concepts.definition: Immersion is the objective, quantifiable degree to which a virtual reality system projects stimuli onto the sensory receptors of users in an extensive, matching, surrounding, vivid, interactive, and plot-informing way.

defining_facts.text: Immersion in virtual reality (VR) means that the user's senses are blocked so that the user receives no input from the real-world environment and receives input only from the virtual world.

From a systems point of view, virtual reality (VR) systems are broadly categorized into non-immersive, semi-immersive, and fully immersive systems because market applications offer varying degrees of immersion rather than all being fully immersive.

Semi-immersive virtual reality (VR) is in between non-immersive and fully immersive VR, giving the user a partial immersive experience by blocking some but not all senses; for example, the eyes may be blocked while ears and skin remain exposed to real-world signals.

Semi-immersive virtual reality (VR) systems are the most cost-effective and commonly used form of VR, and most commercial immersive applications are semi-immersive because they give partial immersion while leaving the user free to sense the real world.

A fully immersive virtual reality (VR) system completely blocks the user's ability to sense the real world by blocking all senses, so the user senses only the things happening in the virtual world, feels physically present in it, and has the user's sense of reality replaced by virtual realism.

Among virtual reality (VR) systems, fully immersive systems are the costliest and commercially rare because they are difficult to afford, while semi-immersive and non-immersive systems are more common.

In virtual reality (VR), headsets or display devices present two-dimensional (2D) images, but stereoscopic vision makes the user perceive them as three-dimensional (3D) objects and space, which is immersion.

In the definition originally proposed by Slater and Wilbur, immersion is the objective degree to which a virtual reality (VR) system and application projects stimuli onto the sensory receptors of users in a way that is extensive, matching, surrounding, vivid, interactive, and plot-informing.

Extensive, as a quality of immersion, refers to the range of sensory modalities presented to the user, with examples including visual, auditory, physical force perception, smell, taste, and touch, and the more sensory organs are stimulated by computer-provided stimuli, the more extensive the immersion is.

Matching, as a quality of immersion, refers to congruence between sensory modalities, especially a match between a user's physical movement and movement in the virtual world, such as immediate visual change when the head moves or virtual reflection of walking or hand movement.

Surrounding, as a quality of immersion, is the extent to which cues are panoramic, such as the extent of visual field of view or the extent of auditory source perception, and a wide field of view produces a more surrounding experience than a narrow field of view.

Vivid, as a quality of immersion, refers to the amount of energy stimulated within a particular sensory modality and is related to factors such as resolution, lighting, frame rate, and audio bit rate, with higher resolution or audio bit rate improving visual or auditory perception and making immersion more vivid.

Interactivity, as a quality of immersion, is the user's capability to make changes to the virtual world, receive responses from virtual entities to user actions, and influence future events, not merely one-way interaction.

Plot-informing, as a quality of immersion, means the experience is a scripted story, and the more the user can understand, comprehend, or predict the consequences of actions and the overall story, including its consistent portrayal, dynamic unfolding, and behavior of the world and its entities, the more plot-informing the experience is.
In virtual reality (VR), immersion is the technological issue and presence is the psychological issue.
Immersion is an objective and quantifiable description of what a particular system can provide or does provide, and that description can be measured or comprehended.

Presence can be a function of both the user's subjective experience and a system's immersion, that is the objective or technological experience, so immersion can aid an enhanced perception of presence and is capable of producing presence, but it does not ensure presence.

Presence can be limited by immersion, and the greater the immersion a system or application provides, the greater the potential for a user to feel present in the virtual world, while the lesser the immersive technology provides, the lesser the presence.
Creating a high degree of presence in a virtual reality system requires the system to provide a high degree of immersion, and this requirement is a systemic issue.

concepts.name: sensor
concepts.definition: Sensor is a device that converts an energy source into electrical signals, or, in the human body, an organ that converts a stimulus into neural impulses; in XR hardware it is a tracking device that tracks a user's movements and extracts information from the real world.

defining_facts.text: Virtual reality (VR) hardware has three major components: displays (output devices), sensors (input devices), and computers (processing devices).

In virtual reality (VR) hardware, a sensor or input device is used in a broad sense to mean any tracking device that tracks the user's input and extracts information from the real world, with the discussion restricted to sensors that track the user's movements.
Tracking is also commonly called sensing; tracking is the more popular term, but the devices that enable tracking are more often called sensors than trackers.

The term sensor has two related but structurally different meanings: in a device or system, a sensor is a device that converts an energy source into electrical signals in a circuit; in the human body, human bodily sensors are body organs that convert a stimulus into neural impulses.

concepts.name: usability
concepts.definition: Usability is an explicit measure of how good a system is from the point of view of the user: the extent to which a product can be used by specified users to achieve specified goals with effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction in a specified context of use.

defining_facts.text: Usability is an explicit measure of how good a system is from the point of view of the user.

The International Standards Organization (ISO) 9241-210-2009 standard defines usability as the extent to which a product can be used by specified users to achieve specified goals with effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction in a specified context of use.

The three crucial aspects of the International Standards Organization (ISO) 9241-210-2009 usability definition are that a usable product is intended for a specified group of users rather than everybody, that it supports a specified set of goals rather than every conceivable feature, and that it is designed for a specified context of use rather than all usage scenarios.

The three measures of usability are effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction; effectiveness is whether the user can do what they want to do, efficiency is how fast the user can do what they want to do, and satisfaction is how satisfied the user is when using the system.

concepts.name: human factors
concepts.definition: Human factors is the system-design consideration that requires knowing users’ differing expectations, needs, skills, and how they perceive stimuli, so that suitable input and output can be designed.

defining_facts.text: Human factors in system design requires designers to know the users' characteristics and design the system accordingly, because users who perform the same broad task, such as a traveler or agent and a database administrator obtaining railway ticket information, can have different expectations, needs, and query-language skills, and therefore require different interfaces for providing input, seeing the outcome, and acting on the outcome.

concepts.name: presence
concepts.definition: Presence is a subjective psychological state in which an experience generated by human-made technology is perceived as real, because the user fails to acknowledge the technology's role and perceives computer-generated stimuli as coming from the real world.

defining_facts.text: Presence is the psychological side that captures whether a user perceives the immersive qualities that are generated.

Presence is defined by the International Society for Presence Research, which has had the definition since 2000, as a psychological state or subjective perception in which part or all of an individual's current experience is generated by or filtered through human-made technology, but part or all of the individual's perception fails to accurately acknowledge the role of the technology in the experience.

Presence is a state in which computer-generated stimuli stimulate the user's sensory organs, and the user's perception is as good as perceiving reality because the user cannot distinguish those stimuli from real-world stimuli, so the user perceives them as coming from the real world rather than from a computer.

Presence is a state of consciousness or psychological sense of being in the virtual environment that exists inside the user's mind, has no direct manifestation, is difficult to measure objectively, and therefore requires the user's subjective experience to be taken into account.

Presence can be a function of both the user's subjective experience and a system's immersion, that is the objective or technological experience, so immersion can aid an enhanced perception of presence and is capable of producing presence, but it does not ensure presence.

Presence can be limited by immersion, and the greater the immersion a system or application provides, the greater the potential for a user to feel present in the virtual world, while the lesser the immersive technology provides, the lesser the presence.

The overall goal of any virtual reality system is to create a high degree of presence, that is to make users feel that they are really in the virtual world and unable to distinguish the real world from the virtual world.
Creating a high degree of presence in a virtual reality system requires the system to provide a high degree of immersion, and this requirement is a systemic issue.

The goal of any virtual reality (VR) system is to create a high degree of presence, meaning that people believe they are in the real world while they are actually in a virtual world, and the closer a VR system is to this goal, the better the immersive experience it provides.

Cybersickness (CS) mitigation involves a trade-off between reducing cybersickness and preserving user experience, because mitigation strategies often affect presence or the user's ability to perceive the virtual world, and presence affects user experience.

Mark Weiser's quote that the most profound technologies are those that disappear and presence refer to the same thing: the technological aspect surrounding the user should disappear from the user's perception, and the goal is to build systems that do not make it apparent that the user is using a specialized technological product.

In an Extended Reality (XR) system, the interaction and the perceptual stimuli, the latter being the output generated by the system, are designed to create the best possible illusion of reality, not actual reality, in order to enhance presence, which is a sense of reality as if the user is in the real world.

Presence in a virtual environment requires both reinforcing the virtual experience as believable and developing attachment to that experience, and the auditory experience plays a very important role in increasing presence in the virtual environment.

The key concerns to be addressed in the Majuli Island virtual reality (VR) Tour are capturing both the tangible and intangible aspects of the island's cultural heritage, which is the broader objective, the user experience, specifically the extent to which users feel present in the virtual island, and minimizing the risk of cyber sickness while users explore the island.
Presence is a psychological state of mind that is measured by standard questionnaires.
The QEP questionnaire was used to measure presence, and it is a 2004 revised version of the standard presence questionnaire (PQ).

The presence measure used to evaluate the virtual tour of Majuli Island included involvement, interface quality, adaptation or immersion, and visual fidelity, and tangible and intangible reconstruction fidelity was additionally reported for participants who had previously visited Majuli Island.

The overall user presence ratings for the virtual tour of Majuli Island were involvement mean 5.65 (standard deviation 1.11, coefficient of variation 0.19), interface quality mean 4.37 (standard deviation 1.4, coefficient of variation 0.32), adaptation and immersion mean 5.4 (standard deviation 1.13, coefficient of variation 0.2), and visual fidelity mean 5.79 (standard deviation 0.93, coefficient of variation 0.16).

The presence ratings for participants who had previously visited Majuli Island were tangible and intangible reconstruction fidelity mean 5.68 (standard deviation 1, coefficient of variation 0.177), involvement mean 5.83 (standard deviation 1.05, coefficient of variation 0.18), interface quality mean 4.72 (standard deviation 1.36, coefficient of variation 0.33), adaptation or immersion mean 5.61 (standard deviation 1.15, coefficient of variation 0.22), and visual fidelity mean 5.94 (standard deviation 0.93, coefficient of variation 0.15).

The overall presence results for the virtual tour of Majuli Island were summarized as good presence, meaning that users felt reasonably well located within the virtual environment while virtually exploring Majuli Island.

concepts.name: cybersickness
concepts.definition: Cybersickness (CS) is a condition primarily relevant to virtual reality that may be caused by multiple internal and external factors and in which a user may experience symptoms such as nausea, dizziness, headache, or disorientation.

defining_facts.text: Cybersickness (CS), also known in the literature as visually induced motion sickness (VIMS), is a condition that can affect individuals when they interact with virtual reality (VR) technology and is primarily relevant to virtual reality.

A large number of symptoms may indicate the onset of cybersickness (CS) or cybersickness itself, and common ones include nausea, headache, excessive sweating, dryness of mouth, fullness of stomach, vomiting or a tendency to vomit, dizziness, disorientation, fatigue, and strange hand-eye coordination in which coordination does not happen in the expected way, so if one or more of these symptoms occur during a virtual reality (VR) experience, cybersickness can be assumed to be happening or going to happen.
Cybersickness (CS) can be caused by many factors, not by a single factor.

Reducing the impact of cybersickness (CS) is very important for usability and acceptability of virtual reality (VR) systems because it greatly enhances overall user experience and makes virtual reality applications more appealing to a wider range of people.

Another possible outcome of generally inconsistent virtual reality stimulation is that the body may not be able to adapt, causing increased fatigue or headaches, and this non-adaptation may lead to cyber sickness, that is, dizziness, nausea, or a large set of different symptoms experienced while using virtual reality systems.

A sensory mismatch in a virtual reality (VR) system may be insignificant if the user's brain can adapt, but for other users it can cause cybersickness, with symptoms such as fatigue, headache, dizziness, and nausea.

Cybersickness, also known as visually induced motion sickness (VIMS), is a condition that can affect individuals when they interact with virtual reality (VR), and it is not a single-factor effect because a variety of factors can affect it.

The factors that can induce cybersickness are broadly divided into internal factors, which include the age of the user, the gender of the user, the user's susceptibility to motion sickness, the physical condition of the user, and the emotional condition of the user, and external factors, which include hardware factors such as display resolution, latency, latency jitter, type of display, and type of input, and virtual reality (VR) content factors such as visual motion, means of locomotion, field of view, type of content, duration, and visual complexity.

Finding feasible solutions to reduce the impact of cybersickness while a user is experiencing virtual reality (VR) is important because it is supposed to greatly enhance overall user experience and make VR more appealing to a wider range of people.

Cybersickness mitigation strategies often come at the cost of presence because reducing cybersickness may make the user feel more in an artificial environment than in a real environment and less likely to obtain a proper immersive experience.

concepts.name: extended reality system
concepts.definition: An Extended reality system is an interactive system that comprises hardware, an XR engine as middleware, and the application layer, in which input devices track the user's actions and positions, send them as input data, the data is processed to render an environment, and output devices stimulate the user's senses.

defining_facts.text: Extended Reality (XR) systems are highly interactive like other interactive systems, and consideration of human factors is important to understand how easily a user can provide input and perceive output.
An Extended Reality (XR) system comprises hardware, the middleware that is the XR engine, and the application layer.

In an Extended Reality (XR) system, the user's actions and positions are tracked by input devices and sent as input data; the input data is processed and the environment is rendered; the XR engine, as middleware, uses hardware resources to generate output data; and output devices stimulate the user's senses with that output.

In an Extended Reality (XR) system, interaction design and modeling of user input should follow a user-centered design approach so that the user can provide input data seamlessly, effectively, and easily.

In an Extended Reality (XR) system, perceptual design and modeling of output requires a user-centered design approach because it is crucial to ensure that generated output stimuli match the user's perception of them, so that the user can perceive and understand the output easily.

concepts.name: interactive system
concepts.definition: Interactive system is a system in which interaction takes place between the computer or system and the user, a lay person who is not necessarily a technology expert and who wants to use the system rather than understand how it works.

defining_facts.text: Interactive computing systems, or interactive systems, are systems in which interaction takes place between the computer or system and the user.
In interactive systems, the user is a lay person or layman user who is not necessarily a technology expert and who wants to use the system rather than understand how the system works.
Designers of interactive systems that are intended to be used by laypersons should not force users to learn the underlying technology or understand the relevant technical terms.

never_defined.name: virtual object
never_defined.definition: A virtual object is an object that does not exist in the real world and can be seen in a virtual world or added to the real world so that it appears to coexist with real objects.

never_defined.name: hardware
never_defined.definition: Hardware is a part of an extended reality (XR) system, including input devices, output devices, processing devices, central processing units, graphics processing units, and memory.

never_defined.name: frame rate
never_defined.definition: Frame rate is the speed, or temporal resolution, at which display pixels change, and in immersive environments higher frame rates are preferred so that motion is perceived smoothly without jitter.

never_defined.name: stimulus
never_defined.definition: Stimulus is a particular input that activates the receptors of a sense organ and is converted into neural impulses. In virtual reality, output devices generate it to affect the user's sense organs. For human senses it can be electromagnetic energy, air pressure waves, tissue distortion, gravity or acceleration, or chemical composition.

never_defined.name: input
never_defined.definition: Input is one of the three major hardware components of a virtual reality (VR) system and, in XR systems, the data that the user provides to interact with the system.

never_defined.name: ear
never_defined.definition: The ear is the sense organ for the auditory sense.

never_defined.name: motion
never_defined.definition: Motion is perceived in a virtual world with respect to the degrees of freedom that are supported.

never_defined.name: gravity
never_defined.definition: Gravity is one stimulus for the balance sense and what makes dropped objects accelerate toward the ground in virtual-world physics.

never_defined.name: illusion of reality
never_defined.definition: Illusion of reality is the best possible sense of reality, not actual reality, created by an XR system's interaction and perceptual stimuli to enhance presence, and creating it is especially crucial in virtual reality.

never_defined.name: perceptual system
never_defined.definition: The perceptual system is the user's system that a VR system can fool into believing the virtual system is the familiar real world.

never_defined.name: artificial stimulation
never_defined.definition: Artificial stimulation is the sensory signals that virtual reality generally provides to the brain, inconsistent with the user's real-life experiences and behavior.

never_defined.name: biological mechanism
never_defined.definition: A biological mechanism is a mechanism in human bodies and sensory organs that evolved over a long period in a natural environment and is affected by artificial stimulation in virtual reality.

never_defined.name: physiology
never_defined.definition: Physiology is one part of human perception, along with experience stored in long-term memory, and, for perceptual psychology, a basic human-body topic involving sense organs, neural pathways, and their connections to the brain.

never_defined.name: long-term memory
never_defined.definition: Long-term memory is a part of human memory that stores experience or knowledge used to interpret sensory input.

never_defined.name: sensory input
never_defined.definition: Sensory input is the real-time input in perceptual processing that is combined with long-term memory to produce an interpretation of a stimulus.

never_defined.name: adaptation
never_defined.definition: Adaptation is a possible outcome of generally inconsistent virtual reality stimulation, in which the body adapts to the new stimuli.

never_defined.name: non-adaptation
never_defined.definition: Non-adaptation is the body's inability to adapt to generally inconsistent virtual reality stimulation, which can cause increased fatigue or headaches and may lead to cyber sickness, such as dizziness, nausea, or other symptoms.

never_defined.name: video resolution
never_defined.definition: Video resolution is the amount needed to avoid seeing pixels in a virtual world or virtual object.

never_defined.name: point of view
never_defined.definition: Point of view is the view in a virtual world for which the user's head should appear at the proper height.

never_defined.name: virtual sound
never_defined.definition: Virtual sound is a sound in a virtual world that perceptual psychology considers when asking where it appears to come from.

never_defined.name: neural pathway
never_defined.definition: A Neural pathway is part of the basic physiology of the human body that perceptual psychology requires knowledge of.

never_defined.name: brain
never_defined.definition: The brain is the part of the human body that receives neural impulses from sense organs and neural pathways, processes them into touch perception, and can send messages back for corrective motor actions.

never_defined.name: energy source
never_defined.definition: An energy source is what a sensor in a device or system converts into electrical signals in a circuit.

never_defined.name: electrical signal
never_defined.definition: Electrical signal is a signal that can be produced in a circuit when a sensor in a device or system converts an energy source, and that can be passed across a synapse between neurons.

never_defined.name: circuit
never_defined.definition: A circuit is a part of a device or system in which electrical signals are present.

never_defined.name: neural impulse
never_defined.definition: A neural impulse is what a sense organ transmits through a neural network to the brain after converting a stimulus.

never_defined.name: electromagnetic energy
never_defined.definition: Electromagnetic energy is the stimulus for vision that activates the eyes' photoreceptors in the frequency range of visible light.

never_defined.name: air pressure wave
never_defined.definition: An air pressure wave is the stimulus for the auditory sense.

never_defined.name: tissue distortion
never_defined.definition: Tissue distortion is the stimulus for the sense of touch.

never_defined.name: skin
never_defined.definition: Skin is a sense organ for touch that has epidermis, dermis, and hypodermis layers, with touch receptors embedded in the epidermis and dermis.

never_defined.name: muscle
never_defined.definition: Muscle is a sense organ for touch that contains muscle spindles and is connected to bones by tendons.

never_defined.name: acceleration
never_defined.definition: Acceleration is a stimulus for the balance sense and is reported by visual input, with kinesthesis providing information on it during movement.

never_defined.name: vestibular organ
never_defined.definition: A vestibular organ is a sense organ for the balance sense.

never_defined.name: chemical composition
never_defined.definition: Chemical composition is the stimulus for taste and smell, the senses whose chemoreceptors provide signals based on it.

never_defined.name: mouth
never_defined.definition: Mouth is the sense organ for taste.

never_defined.name: nose
never_defined.definition: The nose is the sense organ for smell.

never_defined.name: vibration
never_defined.definition: Vibration is used as a typical form of force feedback to provide touch sensation in XR systems.

never_defined.name: gravitational force
never_defined.definition: Gravitational force is a force sensed by mechanoreceptors in the auditory, touch, and balance senses.

never_defined.name: temperature
never_defined.definition: Temperature is what thermoreceptors detect as changes in the sense of touch.

never_defined.name: tongue
never_defined.definition: Tongue is where chemoreceptors for taste are located.

never_defined.name: nasal passage
never_defined.definition: A nasal passage is the location in which smell relies on chemoreceptors that provide signals based on the chemical composition of matter.

never_defined.name: physiology of the senses
never_defined.definition: Physiology of the senses is a part of perceptual psychology.
